idiom_name: BigInt minor units plus Intl.NumberFormat at the edge
implementation_notes: JavaScript has no decimal primitive - number is an IEEE-754 double - so money has to be an integer count of minor units: BigInt since ES2020, or a safe-integer number below 2**53, together with the ISO 4217 code and the exponent looked up per currency rather than assumed to be two. That replaces the classic Money class with a plain immutable object, arithmetic helpers that throw on currency mismatch, BigInt's truncating division for allocation with an explicit leftover pass, and Intl.NumberFormat for display from an exact decimal string, since it already knows each currency's minor-unit count. A method-carrying class is still justified when a team prefers that syntax, but the representation must stay integer.
pitfalls: JSON.stringify throws on BigInt, which is a deliberate forcing function: the wire format (minor-unit integer or decimal string) has to be chosen explicitly.
Calling Number(bigint) or doing float maths anywhere reimports the whole bug: 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3 and integers above 2**53 are no longer exact.
BigInt division truncates toward zero, so allocating negative amounts needs a sign-aware remainder pass.
Mixing BigInt and Number in one expression throws a TypeError at runtime, which surfaces late if the boundary is not typed.

variants.name: dinero.js value objects with a pluggable calculator
variants.idiom_name: dinero.js v2 (immutable objects, number or bigint calculator)
variants.implementation_notes: dinero.js supplies the value type as a library: an amount in minor units plus a currency object carrying base and exponent, a pluggable calculator (number by default, bigint through dinero.js/bigint) and pure functions such as add, multiply, allocate and toDecimal instead of operators. It deliberately has no divide and no percentage, because integer division loses minor units - allocation is the supported operation, which encodes Fowler's argument in an API. Choose it when the team wants the rules packaged and tested; stay with plain BigInt when no dependency may enter the bundle.
pitfalls: The default number calculator is bounded by 2**53, and large amounts need the bigint entry point with its matching bigint currency definitions.
transformScale truncates by default when reducing scale, so a rounding mode has to be passed explicitly.
Currencies are ISO 4217 snapshots inside the package, so the version must be pinned when an exponent matters.
